page: Hetzner Cloud cpx31 is a virtual instance built on the QEMU hypervisor within the Regular Purpose family. It provides 4 shared vCPUs on an AMD EPYC processor running at 2.0 GHz using the x86_64 architecture, alongside 8.0 GB of system memory. Storage is provisioned locally with a bundled 160 GB NVMe SSD, while dedicated graphics acceleration is not included. Complimentary public IPv4 addresses are not allocated by default.

Computational benchmarks show strong single-core performance on stress-ng at 2,681.88, while multi-core stress-ng reaches 10,668.13 within the average tier. Geekbench scoring indicates mid-tier capability, yielding 1,463 for single-core and 4,741 for multi-core evaluations. Memory subsystem throughput reaches 60.53 GB/sec for uncached large-block reads and 41.80 GB/sec for uncached writes, although the PassMark memory benchmark reflects lower-tier results. Multi-threaded bzip3 decompression, Clang software compilation, Redis SET operations, and static web serving throughput also register in lower benchmark tiers.

The 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM configuration offers a dense compute allocation on shared hardware, providing cost efficiency for workloads that do not demand sustained dedicated cores. Tradeoffs include shared CPU contention during peak loads and constrained memory per core at roughly 1.95 GB. Hetzner Cloud cpx31 is suited for lightweight containerized services, CI/CD runners, build tasks, and non-critical development environments.
description: Hetzner Cloud cpx31 is a virtual server featuring 4 shared vCPUs on an AMD EPYC processor operating at 2.0 GHz with x86_64 architecture. The system integrates 8.0 GB of memory and includes a bundled 160 GB local NVMe SSD without discrete GPU hardware or bundled IPv4 addresses. Benchmark assessments demonstrate strong single-core compute performance in stress-ng tests alongside middle-tier multi-core execution in both Geekbench and PassMark. However, memory performance and data-heavy tasks such as multi-threaded decompression, software compilation, and Redis operations fall into lower performance quartiles. The 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio provides balanced resource density on shared hardware, offering cost efficiency for entry-level computational duties while presenting tradeoffs in memory capacity and potential shared CPU contention. This configuration aligns with continuous integration pipelines, batch utility scripts, microservices, and development environments requiring local fast NVMe storage.
